en: Dhātupāṭhavilāsinī.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
To the Perfectly Self-Awakened Sun, who has bestowed the light of full enlightenment.
I bow to him who, like the sun, awakens the multitude of lotuses that are people;
I pay homage to that Sage who, having appeared in the world, has rightly dispelled the darkness of the world with the light of the True Dhamma.
I pay homage to that Buddha, who is strewn with the fragrance of virtue,
the great ship of the True Dharma, who grows from the ocean of the Saṅgha, and who delights all living beings.
Having paid homage to my teacher named Padumārāma, I am his disciple.
Relying upon the Pāḷi, for whom am I [fit] to compose this *Dhātupāṭhavilāsini*,
which delights in the method of the Teacher’s arrival?
It was composed by Sajjana in the village known as Mūkalanga.
A resident of the monastery named Suvisuddhārāma was the Elder Padhāna; he was grateful and of peaceful conduct.
That elder, named Guṇālaṅkāra, delighted in the lineage of the elders.
Having approached me, my friend Vaṅkamānasa entreated me, saying:
"When I become a Buddha in the world, you shall be my attendant.
"I will attain greatness myself—what need is there to speak of another? he said.
The *appa* affix occurs after roots belonging to the *bhūvādi* class when expressing a pure active voice (*suddhakattukriyā*),
being dependent on all verbal roots (*sabbadhātuka*).
It is employed in connection with the agent (*kattunā*) and stands precisely in relation to the primary action (*appadhāniye*).
This verse serves as an illustration of how [the suffix] *kiraya* is established within the Teaching (*sāsana*).
For the most part, only the verbal noun (*karaṇa-vacana*) is seen;
this statement was made with reference to the instances where the causative (*kārita*) occurs in the verb (*ākhyāta*).
The wise one, skilled in application, having brought forward such phrases as "Na nāme kārataṭṭhānaṃ bodhetā" and so forth,
as well as "Sunakhehipi khādāpenti" and so on, should explain them.
It has been stated in brief by means of the term *paccanta*;
the connection of the word *bhūyate* indicates the sense of "becoming. In the text of the *Niddesa*, it is said:
"form becomes (*vihoti*), it is made to become (*vihavīyati*)."
Thus, from the perspective of [the Buddha’s] vision, the first-person singular pronoun is firm—
just as it was spoken by the Sage in the Dhajagga Sutta; and furthermore,
from the perspective of the Pāli text itself, it will be abandoned.
Just as from the bodies of great seers through the power of their perfections, the production of fire occurs—
not by means of words such as "Sakka" and so forth— but rather through direct perception,
so too is the application of the three types of persons [to the stages] by means of personal realization alone.
Whether in the singular or the plural,
it should be understood that our acceptance [of the forms] applies to the *parassapada* and other such endings.
The so-called *bhāve* (passive) and *kriyā* (intransitive) verb forms are extremely difficult to discern within the Pāḷi texts.
Therefore, the means for grasping that [verb] has been stated by me thus far.
That which possesses three tenses, three persons, and three voices, and which expresses three agents,
having three genders and two numbers— that is called a verb (ākhyāta).
Proclaimed is the ocean whose churning produces waves of verbal roots, whose water is the suffixes (*dhātu*),
whose moving fish are the conjugational classes (*vikaraṇa-gama-kāla*),
and whose banks are the divisions of elision (*lopa*), phonetic markers (*anubandha*), and sandhi (*raya-mattha-vibhāga*).
The wise, the seers, cross over by means of the various ships of their own intelligence.
Eye (cakkhu), eye-organ (akkhi), nayana, netta, locana, diṭṭhi, dassana,
pekkhana, acchi, and pamha— these, together with the eyelashes (pakhuma), are so called.
“Exiled from his own kingdom, having gone to another country, one should build a great granary in order to ward off harsh words.
This is an ancient saying, O Incomparable One; it was not like this today.
They blame those who remain silent, they blame those who speak much, and they blame even those who speak in moderation;
there is no one in the world who is not blamed—
just as a frontier city, though guarded both within and without, is still assailed by its enemies.
Thus, "Guard yourself; do not let the opportune moment pass you by.
Fie on that poisonous life for the sake of which I shall vomit again what I have already vomited; death is better for me than such a life.
A man indeed plunders as long as he has the means;
but when others plunder him, being himself plundered, he in turn plunders them.
Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path of death.
"The heedful do not die; those who are heedless are as if dead.
Thus spoke the one named Ñāṇavimalatissa, the leader of the Mahāsaṅgha, who brought the Mon lineage here and established it in this island.
He was his chief disciple, an expert in the Pāḷi and its commentaries,
renowned as Dhammadhāra, the master of the Great Saṅgha;
you were his principal disciple, likewise skilled in the Dhamma and the Suttas.
The great elder Ñāṇānanda was as well-known as the moon;
the poet Vimalasāratissa, known by that name, was the great presiding head of the Saṃgha.
His second disciple was one proficient in the scriptures.
My preceptor, the foremost of elders, was named Padumārāma;
I am his third disciple, devoted to reverence for the training.
And the leader of the Saṅgha, Vimalasāra, is a majestic elephant among elders.
These two great elders, renowned as Padumārāma and Vikhyāta,
received [the teachings] from the presence of the Mahāsaṅgha master Dhammādhāra and from the presence of the great elder Ñāṇānanda.
Among them, indeed, the Great Elder Padumārāma taught me the science of grammar and the Pāḷi commentaries;
after he had passed away, [I studied] prosody, grammar, and so forth.
And from the presence of the great elder Vimalasāra, I received [this teaching]—
from that wise Mahāthera Padumārāma, together with his disciple,
the elder Ñāṇatilaka, who was his equal in wisdom.
Two thousand four hundred and seventy years after the Parinibbāna of the Buddha,
in the delightful month of Jeṭṭha,
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, this *Matisūdanī* was composed.
For the sake of awakening to the meaning of the *Dhātupāṭha*, this *Dhātupāṭhavilāsinī*—
adorned with the ornaments of its virtues and beginning with the *Ādimuddāpana*—
has been offered by me; it is now at the disposal of the ascetic who follows above me.
Guṇānanda was my father, the village headman of Unākuruva;
he was my protector from the very beginning, starting with the binding of the knots.
King Samaññaka was my maternal grandfather, and Macca was my father.
"Oṇīnī, Vīsā, and Sanāmā are my mothers; Senāpati, Ācerā, and Pācerā are likewise my mothers— my father and my mothers,
and all these embodied beings, may they attain Nibbāna."
Thus ends the *Dhātupāṭhavilāsinī*.
